extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and law students (practitioners of patent litigation)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural rules governing when courts of equity will grant, dissolve, or modify injunctions and order accounts of profits in patent infringement cases, including evidentiary practice and defenses (estoppel, acquiescence, public use, laches).

rubrics_metrics.name: Account of profits ordered during pendency
rubrics_metrics.description: An important part of the remedial process in equity is the account of profits made by the defendant. Sometimes an account is ordered to be kept, in lieu of granting or continuing an injunction, and it is always ordered when the injunction is made perpetual, unless the amount would be very small.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordered to secure that the plaintiff, if ultimately entitled, can receive full amends while the defendant continues to use the invention; especially appropriate where defendant might make new contracts if account deferred. Also ordered if injunction dissolved because it would cause irreparable injury to defendant's business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account when validity fully established; scope
rubrics_metrics.description: When the validity of the patent is fully established, an account will be ordered of all the profits made by the defendant, to be taken by a master; and if the patent has expired, the account and the injunction will extend to all the articles piratically made during the existence of the patent, though some of them may remain unsold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account normally taken by a master. Covers profits from piratically made articles manufactured during patent term even if unsold at expiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual inspection and appointment of inspectors/viewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes, as a further means of doing justice between the parties, ... the court will order a mutual inspection of the plaintiff's and defendant's works. For this purpose inspectors or viewers are appointed, under the direction of the court, who are to be admitted as witnesses on the trial at law. If the parties do not agree on the persons to be appointed, the court will appoint them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose is to enable the parties, on the trial, to give such evidence as will tend to prove or disprove the fact of infringement. Inspectors are selected under court direction and may testify at trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injunction revival after favorable judgment at law
rubrics_metrics.description: After a trial and judgment at law, in favor of the plaintiff, the injunction will be revived or granted as matter of course.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may, however, examine the regularity/grounds of the law judgment (e.g., to see if there is probable ground for a writ of error) before reviving or refusing to suspend an injunction; practice varies by jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not dissolve injunction for mere technical/formal doubts
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction should not be dissolved merely on account of doubts as to the validity of the patent, which arise from objections to the technical form or signature of the letters, or other acts or omissions of the public officers, and not from any neglect or wrong of the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If doubts relate to clerical or officer mistakes rather than merits of invention, the court should generally preserve the injunction (unless imperative legal principles show letters-patent to be clearly void). Courts should be cautious about dissolving injunctions for mere technical objections, especially where legislative remedies are pending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of defendants who used invention under license/permission
rubrics_metrics.description: A party who has had such use of an invention, under a contract for an annual rent, or other estimated rate of payment, may discontinue the payment, and, if he still use the invention, the patentee may sue him for the rent due, or for an infringement. If an action is brought for the rent, and the defendant is not estopped by the terms of his contract from denying the validity of the patent, the plaintiff cannot recover without giving him an opportunity to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity will treat such defendants like others on injunction questions; if the bill shows rent due by contract, the court will often order the money to be paid into court to await the result of an action at law. Whether the defendant is estopped is critical; undertakings to account and to pay into court are common conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dedication, surrender, or long acquiescence bars equitable relief
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee, after obtaining his patent, dedicates or surrenders it to public use, or acquiesces for a long period in the public use of his invention, without objection, he is not entitled to the aid of a court of equity to protect it; and such acquiescence may amount to complete proof of a dedication or surrender to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must be clearly established by proof. Acquiescence or encouragement of public use—even by the patentee's silence—may amount to abandonment and will justify refusal of injunction even where legal title exists. If patentee intends a qualified surrender, he should give public notice of the nature and extent of the allowance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable 'must not lie by' doctrine with allowance for evidentiary difficulty
rubrics_metrics.description: Although it is a principle of equity, that a patentee must not lie by, and by his silence or acquiescence induce another to go on expending his money and incurring risk, and afterwards, if profit is made, come and claim a share in the profit, without having been exposed to share in the losses; yet delay to institute his proceedings may be explained by the difficulty of getting evidence of the infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delay (laches) can bar equitable relief but may be excused where plaintiffs reasonably could not obtain evidence earlier. Courts weigh whether plaintiff's conduct led defendants to expend and take risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injunction applications in U.S. equity require notice; injunctions are 'special'
rubrics_metrics.description: In all cases of proceedings in equity to restrain the infringement of patents, in the courts of the United States, the injunction can, at no time, be applied for without notice to the adverse party, giving him an opportunity to oppose it; and, therefore, the injunction is always special.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish common vs special injunctions; because notice is required, plaintiffs must prepare affidavits and evidence to support the application when defendants appear or answer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavits required to show title and infringement when answer filed
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the injunction is applied for before an answer has been filed, the plaintiff, in addition to the allegations in his bill, must read affidavits to show his title, and the fact of infringement, especially if the defendant appears and offers evidence against the one or the other; and these affidavits should, in strictness, cover the issuing of the patent, the novelty of the invention, and all other facts necessary to the title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the defendant attacks the title by affidavit, the plaintiff must support the bill with auxiliary proof beyond the sworn bill to make a prima facie right to an injunction. Where the bill itself is sworn and unchallenged, practice may permit less affidavit proof unless defendant files counter-affidavits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility of affidavits after answer—judicial split and court discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: There has been doubt whether the plaintiff is at liberty to read affidavits in support of his title after an answer denying it. Some judges (McLean) have held the plaintiff may not; others (Woodbury) that the plaintiff may show by counter-evidence that the case differs from the defendant's affidavits or answer. The author inclines to the latter view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantial conflict of decisions exists; courts generally have discretion to look into evidence on both sides to determine whether it is probable the plaintiff will establish his patent and thus whether to grant or withhold an injunction. Analogies to waste cases explain exceptions where irreparable mischief justifies admitting affidavits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court may direct account pending dissolution to preserve plaintiff's remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: If, upon dissolving the injunction, it will direct the defendant to keep an account pending the discontinuance of the injunction, in order that, if it finally turns out that the plaintiff has a valid patent, he may receive amends for the injury occasioned by the resistance to his just demands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When injunction is dissolved for equitable reasons, courts commonly require the defendant to keep an account (and sometimes to deal with it as the court may direct) so the plaintiff can later be compensated if the patent is upheld.
